Plectis

AI-assisted research on eight hard Erdős problems, with Lean proofs, papers and open questions.

Models now write mathematics faster than mathematicians can check it, so each problem here is set out like a funnel, from the Lean map down to one result, to show what is proved, what is not and why.

Explore the mathematics Read the README

Built and maintained by Will Cook. Plectis is Latin for “you weave”.

Selected contributions, including the Erdős #257 variant, have merged into Formal Conjectures. The README links the contribution record.

  1. Erdős #1041Formal statement refuted

    Must some path shorter than 2, where |𝑓| <1|f|<1, join two roots?

    Let 𝑓(𝑧) =∏𝑛𝑖=1(𝑧 −𝑧𝑖) ∈ℂ[𝑧]f(z)=∏i=1n(z−zi)∈C[z] with |𝑧𝑖| <1|zi|<1 for all 𝑖i. Must there always exist a path of length less than 22 in {𝑧 :|𝑓(𝑧)| <1}{z:|f(z)|<1} which connects two of the roots of 𝑓f?

    Erdős problem #1041, as erdosproblems.com/1041 states it

    What it says. Here 𝑓(𝑧) =(𝑧 −𝑧1)(𝑧 −𝑧2)⋯(𝑧 −𝑧𝑛)f(z)=(z−z1)(z−z2)⋯(z−zn) has roots 𝑧1,𝑧2,…,𝑧𝑛z1,z2,…,zn, each less than 1 from 0. The region {|𝑓| <1}{|f|<1} holds every point 𝑧z whose value 𝑓(𝑧)f(z) lies less than 1 from 0, so it holds every root. Any two roots are less than 2 apart; the question is whether some pair is joined by a path shorter than 2 that stays inside the region.

    A complex number 𝑧 =𝑥 +𝑖𝑦z=x+iy is the point (𝑥,𝑦)(x,y) of the plane, and |𝑧| =√𝑥2+𝑦2|z|=x2+y2 is its distance from 0. Likewise |𝑧 −𝑤||z−w| is the distance between the points 𝑧z and 𝑤w, and |𝑧𝑤| =|𝑧| |𝑤||zw|=|z||w|. So |𝑧𝑖| <1|zi|<1 says that every root lies strictly inside the unit circle, the circle of radius 1 about 0.

    Multiplying out gives 𝑓(𝑧) =𝑧𝑛 +⋯f(z)=zn+⋯, and 𝑓(𝑧) =0f(z)=0 exactly when 𝑧z is a root. The rule |𝑧𝑤| =|𝑧| |𝑤||zw|=|z||w| gives

    |𝑓(𝑧)|=|𝑧−𝑧1||𝑧−𝑧2|⋯|𝑧−𝑧𝑛|,|f(z)|=|z−z1||z−z2|⋯|z−zn|,

    the product of the distances from 𝑧z to the roots. The region {𝑧 :|𝑓(𝑧)| <1}{z:|f(z)|<1} is where this product is less than 1, that is, where the value 𝑓(𝑧)f(z) lies within distance 1 of 0. Each root is in it.

    A path is a continuous curve; its length is that of a string laid along it, and it is never less than the straight distance between its ends. For two roots, |𝑧1 −𝑧2| ≤|𝑧1| +|𝑧2| <2|z1−z2|≤|z1|+|z2|<2 (the triangle inequality), so the segment between them is always shorter than 2. The difficulty is that it may leave the region: for 𝑓(𝑧) =𝑧3 −0.993f(z)=z3−0.993, the midpoint of each pair of roots has |𝑓| >1.09|f|>1.09.

    The question is about every such polynomial, of every degree 𝑛 ≥2n≥2: must some pair of distinct roots be joined inside the region by a path shorter than 2? One polynomial with no such pair answers it no. Erdős, Herzog and Piranian asked it in 1958; Pendyala proved that such a path always exists in degree four.

    “Formal statement refuted” means this. Formal Conjectures, a public library of open problems written in the proof language Lean, states the question as a precise formula; ani’s polynomial answers it no, and the paper’s Lean sources prove this. Whether the formula matches the 1958 wording has not had independent human review.

    An example. Take the roots 0.9 and −0.9−0.9, so 𝑓(𝑧) =(𝑧 −0.9)(𝑧 +0.9) =𝑧2 −0.81f(z)=(z−0.9)(z+0.9)=z2−0.81. At a real number 𝑡t between the roots, 𝑓(𝑡) =𝑡2 −0.81f(t)=t2−0.81 lies between −0.81−0.81 and 0, so |𝑓(𝑡)| ≤0.81 <1|f(t)|≤0.81<1. The straight segment stays in the region and joins the roots with length 1.8, less than 2.

    The same example shows how a path can be forced through a narrow place. The imaginary axis holds the points 𝑖𝑦iy, equally far from both roots, and there 𝑓(𝑖𝑦) =(𝑖𝑦)2 −0.81 = −𝑦2 −0.81f(iy)=(iy)2−0.81=−y2−0.81, so

    |𝑓(𝑖𝑦)|=0.81+𝑦2<1⟺𝑦2<0.19⟺|𝑦|<0.436…|f(iy)|=0.81+y2<1⟺y2<0.19⟺|y|<0.436…

    The region meets the axis only in the points 𝑖𝑦iy with |𝑦| <0.436…|y|<0.436…: call this segment the passage. It is where 𝑓f takes values on the short cut from 𝑓(0) = −0.81f(0)=−0.81 to −1−1; 0 is where 𝑓′(𝑧) =2𝑧f′(z)=2z is zero.

    1. A path from 0.9 to −0.9−0.9 starts with real part 0.9 and ends with real part −0.9−0.9. The real part changes continuously, so it is 0 somewhere: a path inside the region crosses the passage at some 𝑖𝑦iy with 𝑦2 <0.19y2<0.19.
    2. The part from 0.9 to 𝑖𝑦iy is at least the straight distance √0.81+𝑦20.81+y2 (Pythagoras), and so is the part from 𝑖𝑦iy to −0.9−0.9. The path is at least 2√0.81+𝑦220.81+y2 long.
    3. In the passage 0.81 +𝑦2 <10.81+y2<1, so this bound is less than 2√1 =221=2; at 𝑦 =0y=0 it is 1.8, the segment.

    So crossing a passage costs at least the sum of the distances from the two roots to the crossing point. Here both distances are below 1: they are equal and their product is |𝑓(𝑖𝑦)| <1|f(iy)|<1. Every quadratic behaves the same way. A counterexample needs a passage off to one side, where the two distances add up to more than 2.

    The crux. In ani’s degree-seven example the roots sit 10−9610−96 inside the unit circle, and the region is seven petals with one root in each, nearly touching at the centre. Only two petals join, through a tiny passage 0.82 ×10−120.82×10−12 from the centre, on the side away from the chord between their roots. Every path between those roots must cross the passage, and their distances to it add up to just over 2.

    So far: a path costs at least its two roots’ distances to the passage it crosses. Next: a region where only one pair can be joined, through a passage where those distances add up to more than 2.

    1. Seven petals. If 𝑧 =𝑟(cos⁡𝜃 +𝑖sin⁡𝜃)z=r(cos⁡θ+isin⁡θ) then 𝑧7 =𝑟7(cos⁡7𝜃 +𝑖sin⁡7𝜃)z7=r7(cos⁡7θ+isin⁡7θ). Points within 1 of the number 1 have positive real part, so |𝑧7 −1| <1|z7−1|<1 forces cos⁡7𝜃 >0cos⁡7θ>0: 𝜃θ lies within 90∘/7 ≈12.9∘90∘/7≈12.9∘ of a multiple of 360∘/7 ≈51.4∘360∘/7≈51.4∘. The region of 𝑧7 −1z7−1 is seven petals, one round each root, separated by empty wedges and meeting at 0, which is outside: |07 −1| =1|07−1|=1.
    2. Changes near the centre. ani moves the roots in to distance 𝜌 =1 −10−96ρ=1−10−96 and adds terms such as 10−48𝑎𝑧310−48az3, 10−60𝑏𝑧210−60bz2 and 10−72𝑐𝑧10−72cz (with 𝑎,𝑏,𝑐a,b,c a few hundred). At |𝑧| =10−12|z|=10−12 these and 𝑧7z7 are all 10−8410−84 times their coefficients, so there they decide how the petals meet.
    3. Six pieces. A piece holding 𝑘k roots contains 𝑘 −1k−1 zeros of 𝑓′f′ (Ebenfelt, Khavinson and Shapiro). Those six zeros lie within 3.6 ×10−123.6×10−12 of 0, and only one, 𝑃P, has |𝑓| <1|f|<1. So one piece holds two roots, A and B, 1.95 apart, and five hold one each.
    4. The passage. On the piece of A and B, 𝑓f takes each value of the unit disc twice, as in the example. Cut the disc of values from 𝑓(𝑃)f(P) out to the unit circle: the points with values on the cut form the passage, and the rest splits into a half holding A and a half holding B. So a path from A to B crosses the passage, which lies within 2.7 ×10−162.7×10−16 of 𝑃P (Lemma 2.1).
    5. The distances. 𝑃P lies 𝑑 =0.823 ×10−12d=0.823×10−12 straight up from 0, at 64.3∘64.3∘ and 141.4∘141.4∘ to the directions of A and B. By the cosine rule, |𝐴 −𝑃|2 =𝜌2 +𝑑2 −2𝜌𝑑cos⁡64.3∘|A−P|2=ρ2+d2−2ρdcos⁡64.3∘, and as 𝑑d is tiny, |𝐴 −𝑃| ≈𝜌 −0.434𝑑|A−P|≈ρ−0.434d; likewise |𝐵 −𝑃| ≈𝜌 +0.782𝑑|B−P|≈ρ+0.782d. The sum is 2𝜌 +0.348𝑑 ≈2 +0.286 ×10−122ρ+0.348d≈2+0.286×10−12.

    A crossing point within 2.7 ×10−162.7×10−16 of 𝑃P lowers that sum by at most 5.4 ×10−165.4×10−16, so every path joining two roots inside the region is longer than 2; the paper’s exact rational bounds give more than 2 +1.4 ×10−132+1.4×10−13.     The interesting resultCounterexample

    A degree-seven counterexample to the formal #1041 statement

    On the hatched region ani’s polynomial has |𝑓| <1|f|<1; its seven zeros lie inside the unit circle, less than 2 apart. Magnified, the petals almost touch at five places and join through a passage at a sixth: only A and B share a piece. A route through 𝑧z is at least |𝑧 −𝐴| +|𝑧 −𝐵||z−A|+|z−B| long; at the centre it is 2 −2 ⋅10−962−2⋅10−96. Routes no longer than 2 stay inside the ellipse where that sum is 2; close up it is a line, and the passage lies beyond it. Closer, the whole passage lies in the small circle C, which every route from A to B must enter. Even if travel inside C were free, reaching it from A and B costs more than 2, so every path joining two zeros is longer than 2.

    The zeros of ani’s 𝑓f are 𝑏𝑗 =𝜌𝜁𝑗bj=ρζj, |𝜁𝑗| =1|ζj|=1, 𝜌 =1 −10−96ρ=1−10−96; at the scale of the disc |𝑓| <1|f|<1 cannot be told from |𝑧7 −1| <1|z7−1|<1, and 𝐴 =𝑏3A=b3, 𝐵 =𝑏6B=b6. The windows use 𝑧 =𝜌𝜀𝑤z=ρεw, 𝜀 =10−12ε=10−12, where 𝑓 =𝜌7( −1 +𝜀7𝑄(𝑤))f=ρ7(−1+ε7Q(w)) and the region is Re⁡𝑄 >0Re⁡Q>0 to drawing precision. Of the six critical points of 𝑄Q only 𝑤𝑠 ≈0.823𝑖ws≈0.823i has a critical value inside the unit disc, so five components hold one zero each. The ellipse |𝑧 −𝐴| +|𝑧 −𝐵| =2|z−A|+|z−B|=2 passes within 10−9510−95 of 0 and is, in the window, the line Re⁡((¯𝜁3 +¯𝜁6)𝑤) =0Re⁡((ζ¯3+ζ¯6)w)=0. Lemma 2.1 with (3) puts the whole slit preimage within 𝜌𝜀/3750ρε/3750 of 𝑐𝑠 =𝜌𝜀𝑤𝑠cs=ρεws; as |𝑤𝑠 −4𝑖/5| <1/40|ws−4i/5|<1/40, it lies in 𝐶 :|𝑤 −4𝑖/5| ≤1/10C:|w−4i/5|≤1/10. The root intervals give Im⁡(𝜁3 +𝜁6) < −1/3Im⁡(ζ3+ζ6)<−1/3, so dist⁡(𝐴,𝐶) +dist⁡(𝐵,𝐶) >𝜌(2 +4𝜀/15) −𝜌𝜀/5 =𝜌(2 +𝜀/15) >2dist⁡(A,C)+dist⁡(B,C)>ρ(2+4ε/15)−ρε/5=ρ(2+ε/15)>2. A connected set joining the two zeros reaches C on each of the two inverse sheets, so its one-dimensional Hausdorff measure exceeds 2 (Theorem 1.2; the paper’s own bound is 𝜌(2 +(1431000 −815000)𝜀)ρ(2+(1431000−815000)ε)). C encloses the passage; the passage itself is far narrower than a pixel. This refutes the formal statement, whose match with Erdős’s 1958 wording has not had independent human review.

    There is a monic polynomial 𝑓f with all its zeros in the open unit disc such that every path in |𝑓| <1|f|<1 joining two of its zeros has an image of one-dimensional Hausdorff measure at least 22. The paper’s witness is ani’s polynomial of degree seven.

    Proof idea. In ani’s polynomial two zeros share one component of |𝑓| <1|f|<1, and its only critical point inside |𝑓| <1|f|<1 sits about 0.82 ×10−120.82×10−12 from the centre, where its distances to those zeros add up to more than 2 +10−132+10−13. A connected set joining the two zeros must reach a tiny disc around that point from each of them, so its measure exceeds 22. Every other component holds one zero.

    Boundary. This refutes the Formal Conjectures statement. Correspondence with Erdős’s 1958 wording has not received independent human review.

    Lean proofComparator checkPaper §2In the map

    Lean is a programming language for mathematics: a theorem is written in it and a computer checks every step of its proof. Comparator is a separate checking tool: it tests the Lean proof against a statement of the theorem written down on its own, so a proof of a weaker or different statement would fail.

  2. Erdős #257Open

    Is the sum of 1/(2𝑛 −1)1/(2n−1) over every infinite set of 𝑛n irrational?

    Let 𝐴 ⊆ℕA⊆N be an infinite set. Is ∑𝑛∈𝐴12𝑛−1∑n∈A12n−1 irrational?

    Erdős problem #257, as erdosproblems.com/257 states it

    What it says. Take any infinite set 𝐴A of positive whole numbers, for example the primes 2,3,5,7,…2,3,5,7,…, and for each 𝑛n in 𝐴A form 1/(2𝑛 −1)1/(2n−1): 1/31/3 for 𝑛 =2n=2, 1/71/7 for 𝑛 =3n=3, 1/311/31 for 𝑛 =5n=5. Add these over all of 𝐴A. The question is whether the total is always irrational, never a fraction 𝑝/𝑞p/q of whole numbers.

    Read the statement symbol by symbol. ℕN is the set of positive whole numbers 1,2,3,…1,2,3,…, and 𝐴 ⊆ℕA⊆N says that 𝐴A is a collection of them. Infinite means the collection never ends: the even numbers 2,4,6,8,…2,4,6,8,… form an infinite set, while {2,3,5}{2,3,5} is finite. For each 𝑛n in 𝐴A the term is 1/(2𝑛 −1)1/(2n−1). The denominators 2𝑛 −12n−1 for 𝑛 =1,2,3,4,5,…n=1,2,3,4,5,… are 1,3,7,15,31,…1,3,7,15,31,…, so the terms are 1,13,17,115,131,…1,13,17,115,131,…. The sum adds the terms for the members of 𝐴A only; for the even numbers it is 13 +115 +163 +⋯13+115+163+⋯.

    Every such sum adds up to a definite number, at most 2. Indeed 2𝑛 −1 ≥2𝑛−12n−1≥2n−1, since the difference is 2𝑛−1 −1 ≥02n−1−1≥0, so each term is at most 1/2𝑛−11/2n−1, and 1 +12 +14 +⋯ =21+12+14+⋯=2.

    Irrational means the sum cannot be written as 𝑝/𝑞p/q with 𝑝p and 𝑞q whole numbers. The question asks this of every infinite 𝐴A: a single infinite set whose sum is a fraction would answer it no. Finite sets are left out because their sums are always fractions: {2,3}{2,3} gives 13 +17 =102113+17=1021. Each 2𝑛 −12n−1 is odd, so a finite sum always has an odd denominator, and no finite set sums to 1212. Whether some infinite set sums to exactly 1212 is unknown.

    A proof must therefore work for an infinite set about which nothing else is known, and a sum of infinitely many terms cannot be computed exactly. What it needs is a property that every fraction 𝑝/𝑞p/q has and that the sum can be shown to lack.

    An example. In binary 1/7 =0.001001001…1/7=0.001001001…, a 1 at every third place; likewise 1/(2𝑛 −1)1/(2n−1) has a 1 at every 𝑛nth place. Adding these rows for every 𝑛n, place 𝑘k receives one 1 for each divisor of 𝑘k: place 6 receives four, from 1, 2, 3 and 6. Erdős proved this total, 1 +1/3 +1/7 +⋯ =1.60669…1+1/3+1/7+⋯=1.60669…, irrational in 1948; over the primes, 1/3 +1/7 +1/31 +⋯ =0.51694…1/3+1/7+1/31+⋯=0.51694… is irrational by Tao and Teräväinen.

    Why the 1s fall at every 𝑛nth place: dividing top and bottom by 2𝑛2n gives 12𝑛−1 =2−𝑛1−2−𝑛12n−1=2−n1−2−n, the sum of a geometric series whose first term and ratio are both 2−𝑛2−n:

    12𝑛−1=2−𝑛+2−2𝑛+2−3𝑛+⋯12n−1=2−n+2−2n+2−3n+⋯

    Each power 2−𝑘𝑛2−kn is a binary 1 at place 𝑘𝑛kn. For 𝑛 =3n=3, 17 =18 +164 +1512 +⋯ =0.001001001…17=18+164+1512+⋯=0.001001001… in binary.

    The crux multiplies every term by 2𝑁 −12N−1. With 𝑁 =6N=6 the multiplier is 63, and the terms for 𝑛 =1n=1 to 77 give

    631=63,633=21,637=9,6363=1,631=63,633=21,637=9,6363=1, 6315=4+315,6331=2+131,63127=0+63127.6315=4+315,6331=2+131,63127=0+63127.

    The exponents 1, 2, 3 and 6 divide 6 and give whole numbers: 21 wholes from 𝑛 =2n=2, nine from 𝑛 =3n=3. Binary shows why. Multiplying 17 =0.001001001…17=0.001001001… by 64 moves the point six places right, to 1001.001001… =9 +171001.001001…=9+17, and the digits after the point are the same as before because 6 is a multiple of the period 3. Subtracting the original 1717 leaves 637 =647 −17 =9637=647−17=9 exactly.

    For 𝑛 =4n=4 the period does not fit into 6. Moving 115 =0.000100010001…115=0.000100010001… six places gives 100.0100010001… =4 +415100.0100010001…=4+415: the 1s after the point sit two places out of step, and 6415 −115 =4 +3156415−115=4+315 leaves 315315. In general, when 𝑁 =𝑚𝑛 +𝑟N=mn+r with 0 <𝑟 <𝑛0<r<n, the leftover is (2𝑟 −1)/(2𝑛 −1)(2r−1)/(2n−1): 6 =4 +26=4+2 gives 315315 and 6 =5 +16=5+1 gives 131131. Each 𝑛n larger than 𝑁N leaves all of (2𝑁 −1)/(2𝑛 −1)(2N−1)/(2n−1), which is less than 1.

    The crux. If the total 𝑆S were 𝑝/𝑞p/q, multiply it by 2𝑁 −12N−1 and remove the whole part of every term: what is left, Δ(𝑁)Δ(N), would be a positive multiple of 1/𝑞1/q. An 𝑛n in 𝐴A dividing 𝑁N leaves nothing, since its binary pattern repeats after 𝑁N places, so a proof seeks 𝑁N divisible by many members of 𝐴A. The others decide everything: for some sets they leave almost nothing; for an arbitrary infinite 𝐴A no method is known.

    To show that the sum 𝑆S over an infinite 𝐴A is no fraction, suppose 𝑆 =𝑝/𝑞S=p/q with 𝑝,𝑞p,q whole and 𝑞 ≥1q≥1. Fourier proved 𝑒e irrational this way: multiply by a large whole number, remove the whole part, and show the rest is positive yet too small. Here the multiplier is 2𝑁 −12N−1, which makes each term with 𝑛n dividing 𝑁N whole. Removing every term's whole part, 𝐽(𝑁)J(N) in all, leaves

    Δ(𝑁)=(2𝑁−1)𝑆−𝐽(𝑁)=∑𝑛∈𝐴2𝑁mod𝑛−12𝑛−1,Δ(N)=(2N−1)S−J(N)=∑n∈A2Nmodn−12n−1,

    where 𝑁mod𝑛Nmodn is the remainder on dividing 𝑁N by 𝑛n.

    1. If 𝑆 =𝑝/𝑞S=p/q, then Δ(𝑁) =((2𝑁 −1)𝑝 −𝑞𝐽(𝑁))/𝑞Δ(N)=((2N−1)p−qJ(N))/q, a whole number over 𝑞q. Removing any whole number keeps this form; removing exactly the whole parts leaves each term at least 0 and below 1. One whole more would make that term negative.
    2. Δ(𝑁)Δ(N) is never zero: as 𝐴A is infinite, some 𝑛n in 𝐴A exceeds 𝑁N and leaves (2𝑁 −1)/(2𝑛 −1) >0(2N−1)/(2n−1)>0. A finite set can leave zero, as a fraction must: 𝐴 ={2,3}A={2,3} and 𝑁 =6N=6 give 63 ×1021 =3063×1021=30 exactly.

    Let 𝐴A be an infinite set of positive integers and 𝑃P a finite nonempty set of primes. Let ℎ(𝑎)h(a) be the largest divisor of 𝑎a using primes in 𝑃P. If ∑𝑎∈𝐴ℎ(𝑎)𝑎(2ℎ(𝑎)−1)<∞,∑a∈Ah(a)a(2h(a)−1)<∞, then ∑𝑎∈𝐴1𝑏𝑎−1∑a∈A1ba−1 is irrational for every integer 𝑏 ≥2b≥2.

    Does a rational reciprocal sum force Sylvester’s rule?

    Let 𝑎1 <𝑎2 <…a1<a2<… be a sequence of integers such that lim𝑛→∞𝑎𝑛𝑎2𝑛−1 =1limn→∞anan−12=1 and ∑1𝑎𝑛 ∈ℚ∑1an∈Q. Then, for all sufficiently large 𝑛 ≥1n≥1, 𝑎𝑛 =𝑎2𝑛−1 −𝑎𝑛−1 +1an=an−12−an−1+1.

    Erdős problem #243, as erdosproblems.com/243 states it

    What it says. Take increasing whole numbers 𝑎1 <𝑎2 <⋯a1<a2<⋯, each roughly the square of the one before, in the sense that 𝑎𝑛/𝑎2𝑛−1an/an−12 tends to 1, and suppose the reciprocals 1/𝑎1 +1/𝑎2 +⋯1/a1+1/a2+⋯ add up to a fraction. Erdős and Graham asked whether every term from some point on must then be exactly 𝑎2𝑛−1 −𝑎𝑛−1 +1an−12−an−1+1, the rule that builds Sylvester’s sequence.

    Symbol by symbol. 𝑎1 <𝑎2 <⋯a1<a2<⋯ is an infinite list of whole numbers, each larger than the one before; the dots mean it never ends. lim𝑛→∞𝑎𝑛/𝑎2𝑛−1 =1limn→∞an/an−12=1 says that, far enough along the list, each term divided by the square of the term before is as close to 1 as we like. So the terms grow extremely fast, each with about twice as many digits as the one before. ∑1/𝑎𝑛∑1/an means 1/𝑎1 +1/𝑎2 +1/𝑎3 +⋯1/a1+1/a2+1/a3+⋯, which has a finite value because the terms grow so fast, and ∈ℚ∈Q says that value is a fraction 𝑝/𝑞p/q of whole numbers. A number that is no such fraction is called irrational.

    The conclusion is that from some position 𝑁N on, every term is made from the one before by Sylvester’s rule 𝑎𝑛 =𝑎2𝑛−1 −𝑎𝑛−1 +1an=an−12−an−1+1. The terms before position 𝑁N may be anything. Sequences following the rule satisfy both hypotheses (the example shows why). Growth alone does not force the rule: 2,4,16,256,…2,4,16,256,…, each term the square of the one before, has every ratio exactly 1 and breaks it. So the question is whether the rule is the only way for such a sum to be a fraction: must every sequence with this growth that breaks the rule at infinitely many positions have an irrational sum? A proof has to turn one equation about an infinite sum into an exact equation for every late term.

    The statement says “integers”; the short paper writes 1 ≤𝑎11≤a1. This changes nothing. Since 𝑎𝑛/𝑎2𝑛−1an/an−12 tends to 1, every late term is positive, so an increasing list has only finitely many terms below 1. Deleting those terms changes the sum by a fraction, so a fractional sum stays fractional and an irrational one stays irrational, and it changes neither the growth condition nor a conclusion about all late terms.

    An example. Sylvester’s sequence 2,3,7,43,1807,…2,3,7,43,1807,… starts at 2 and follows the rule. Its partial sums fall short of 1 by 1/2,1/6,1/42,1/1806,…1/2,1/6,1/42,1/1806,…; for instance 1/2 +1/3 +1/7 =41/42 =1 −1/421/2+1/3+1/7=41/42=1−1/42. Each shortfall is one over (next term minus 1), and these shrink to 0, so the sum is exactly 1. The ratios 𝑎𝑛/𝑎2𝑛−1an/an−12 are 3/4,7/9,43/49,1807/1849,…3/4,7/9,43/49,1807/1849,…, tending to 1.

    Why each shortfall is one over (next term minus 1). Sylvester’s rule says 𝑎𝑛+1 −1 =𝑎𝑛(𝑎𝑛 −1)an+1−1=an(an−1). Subtracting over a common denominator gives

    1𝑎𝑛−1−1𝑎𝑛=𝑎𝑛−(𝑎𝑛−1)𝑎𝑛(𝑎𝑛−1)=1𝑎𝑛+1−1.1an−1−1an=an−(an−1)an(an−1)=1an+1−1.

    With numbers, 1/6 −1/7 =1/421/6−1/7=1/42 and 1/42 −1/43 =1/18061/42−1/43=1/1806. Before any term is added the shortfall is 1 =1/(2 −1)1=1/(2−1). Each time 1/𝑎𝑛1/an is added, a shortfall of 1/(𝑎𝑛 −1)1/(an−1) is replaced by 1/(𝑎𝑛+1 −1)1/(an+1−1), so the shortfalls are 1,1/2,1/6,1/42,1/1806,1/3263442,…1,1/2,1/6,1/42,1/1806,1/3263442,…, and each next term is one more than the current denominator. The same steps, started at any term 𝑎𝑁aN from which the rule holds, leave a shortfall 1/(𝑎𝑁+𝑘 −1)1/(aN+k−1) that shrinks to 0, so the tail is

    1𝑎𝑁+1𝑎𝑁+1+1𝑎𝑁+2+⋯=1𝑎𝑁−1.1aN+1aN+1+1aN+2+⋯=1aN−1.

    The terms before do not matter. Starting at 4 gives 4,13,157,24493,…4,13,157,24493,… with sum 1/31/3. The list 5,6,7,43,1807,…5,6,7,43,1807,… breaks the rule twice (after 5 the rule gives 52 −5 +1 =2152−5+1=21, after 6 it gives 31) and follows it from 43 on; its sum is 1/5 +1/6 +1/6 =8/151/5+1/6+1/6=8/15, since the tail from 7 is 1/61/6.

    The growth: dividing the rule by 𝑎2𝑛an2 gives 𝑎𝑛+1/𝑎2𝑛 =1 −1/𝑎𝑛 +1/𝑎2𝑛an+1/an2=1−1/an+1/an2, which tends to 1 as 𝑎𝑛an grows. For instance 43/49 =1 −1/7 +1/4943/49=1−1/7+1/49.

    The crux. If the sum is 𝑝/𝑞p/q, multiply the tail 1/𝑎𝑛 +1/𝑎𝑛+1 +⋯1/an+1/an+1+⋯ by 𝑞 𝑎1𝑎2⋯𝑎𝑛−1qa1a2⋯an−1. The result is a positive whole number 𝐶𝑛Cn, and Sylvester’s rule holds from some point on exactly when 𝐶𝑛Cn stops changing; for his sequence every 𝐶𝑛Cn is 1, as drawn. In a counterexample 𝐶𝑛Cn would grow without bound, rising again and again. The short paper excludes rises of bounded size, and a growth rate that would make 𝐶𝑛Cn grow like 𝑛(𝑛 +1)(𝑛 +2)n(n+1)(n+2).

    Whole numbers from a fraction. As in Fourier’s proof that 𝑒e is irrational, multiply a tail by a well-chosen whole number. Write 𝑥𝑛 =1/𝑎𝑛 +1/𝑎𝑛+1 +⋯xn=1/an+1/an+1+⋯ and 𝐷𝑛 =𝑞 𝑎1⋯𝑎𝑛−1Dn=qa1⋯an−1. Since 𝑥𝑛 =𝑝/𝑞 −1/𝑎1 −⋯ −1/𝑎𝑛−1xn=p/q−1/a1−⋯−1/an−1,

    𝐶𝑛=𝐷𝑛𝑥𝑛=𝑝𝑎1⋯𝑎𝑛−1−𝐷𝑛𝑎1−⋯−𝐷𝑛𝑎𝑛−1,Cn=Dnxn=pa1⋯an−1−Dna1−⋯−Dnan−1,

    and each 𝐷𝑛/𝑎𝑘Dn/ak is whole because 𝑎𝑘ak is a factor of 𝐷𝑛Dn. So 𝐶𝑛Cn is a whole number (Koizumi’s tail numerator), positive because the tail is. Using 𝑥𝑛+1 =𝑥𝑛 −1/𝑎𝑛xn+1=xn−1/an and 𝐷𝑛+1 =𝑎𝑛𝐷𝑛Dn+1=anDn:

    𝐶𝑛+1=𝑎𝑛𝐶𝑛−𝐷𝑛,𝐶𝑛+1−𝐶𝑛=𝐷𝑛((𝑎𝑛−1)𝑥𝑛−1).Cn+1=anCn−Dn,Cn+1−Cn=Dn((an−1)xn−1).

    So 𝐶𝑛Cn stays the same when the tail is exactly 1/(𝑎𝑛 −1)1/(an−1), falls when it is smaller, and rises when it is larger.

    1. The rule from some point on keeps 𝐶𝑛Cn fixed: by the example, every late tail is 1/(𝑎𝑛 −1)1/(an−1).
    2. If 𝐶𝑛 =𝐶𝑛+1 =𝐶𝑛+2 =𝐶Cn=Cn+1=Cn+2=C, then 𝐶 =𝑎𝑛𝐶 −𝐷𝑛C=anC−Dn gives 𝐷𝑛 =(𝑎𝑛 −1)𝐶Dn=(an−1)C, so 𝐷𝑛+1 =𝑎𝑛(𝑎𝑛 −1)𝐶Dn+1=an(an−1)C, and 𝐶 =𝑎𝑛+1𝐶 −𝐷𝑛+1C=an+1C−Dn+1 divided by 𝐶C gives 𝑎𝑛+1 =𝑎2𝑛 −𝑎𝑛 +1an+1=an2−an+1.

    In the drawing, 𝑞 =1q=1 and 𝐶𝑛 =1 ⋅1 =2 ⋅12 =6 ⋅16 =⋯ =1Cn=1⋅1=2⋅12=6⋅16=⋯=1. For 2,4,16,256,65536,…2,4,16,256,65536,… the tail 1/𝑎𝑛 +1/𝑎2𝑛 +1/𝑎4𝑛 +⋯1/an+1/an2+1/an4+⋯ is smaller than the geometric series 1/𝑎𝑛 +1/𝑎2𝑛 +1/𝑎3𝑛 +⋯ =1/(𝑎𝑛 −1)1/an+1/an2+1/an3+⋯=1/(an−1), and for 𝑛 =1,…,5n=1,…,5, 𝑎1⋯𝑎𝑛−1 𝑥𝑛a1⋯an−1xn is 0.816…,0.632…,0.531…,0.501…,0.500007…0.816…,0.632…,0.531…,0.501…,0.500007….     So far: the rule means 𝐶𝑛Cn eventually fixed. In a counterexample 𝐶𝑛Cn keeps changing, each time by at least 1, while 𝐶𝑛+1/𝐶𝑛Cn+1/Cn tends to 1 (it differs from 𝑎2𝑛/𝑎𝑛+1an2/an+1 by at most a fixed multiple of 1/𝑎𝑛1/an). So 𝐶𝑛Cn grows without bound, and since it cannot fall forever, it rises again and again.

    The short paper proves the rule when every rise is at most a fixed size: after cancelling a common factor, no later 𝐶𝑛Cn shares a factor with an earlier term, the Chinese remainder theorem builds, as high as we like, a block of consecutive whole numbers each sharing one, and small rises cannot jump the block.     The interesting resultIrrationality theorem

    A precise 3/n correction to squaring forces irrationality

    Take 8,16,103,5305,…8,16,103,5305,…, where 𝑎2𝑛/𝑎𝑛+1 =1 +3/𝑛 +𝑜(𝑛−3)an2/an+1=1+3/n+o(n−3). If the reciprocals summed to 𝑝/𝑞p/q, every tail, written over 𝑞q times the earlier terms, would have an integer numerator. The cubic 𝑛(𝑛 +1)(𝑛 +2)/6n(n+1)(n+2)/6 grows by exactly 1 +3/𝑛1+3/n; so four rounds of differences of the numerators are integers tending to zero, and the numerators become a cubic. Chebotarev’s theorem and traces in a cubic field leave 2𝑛(𝑛 +1)(𝑛 +2) ±12n(n+1)(n+2)±1; modulo 7 they read 1, 6, 0, 2 or 4, 5, 0, 1. A zero numerator fixes the denominator under it, 5 or 6, and one step earlier the denominator 𝑑d must satisfy 𝑑2 =2d2=2. Only 3 and 4 square to 2. One more step back, 𝑑 +2d+2 must be a square; 5 and 6 are not, so the sum is irrational.

    For every strictly increasing sequence of positive integers with 𝑎2𝑛𝑎𝑛+1=1+3𝑛+𝑜(𝑛−3),an2an+1=1+3n+o(n−3), the reciprocal sum ∑1𝑎𝑛∑1an is irrational.

  4. Erdős #1049Open

    Is 1𝑡−1 +1𝑡2−1 +1𝑡3−1 +⋯1t−1+1t2−1+1t3−1+⋯ irrational for every rational 𝑡 >1t>1?

    Let 𝑡 >1t>1 be a rational number. Is ∑∞𝑛=11𝑡𝑛−1 =∑∞𝑛=1𝜏(𝑛)𝑡𝑛∑n=1∞1tn−1=∑n=1∞τ(n)tn irrational, where 𝜏(𝑛)τ(n) counts the divisors of 𝑛n? A conjecture of Chowla.

    Erdős problem #1049, as erdosproblems.com/1049 states it

    What it says. Take a rational number 𝑡t greater than 1, such as 3/23/2, and add 1/(𝑡 −1) +1/(𝑡2 −1) +1/(𝑡3 −1) +⋯1/(t−1)+1/(t2−1)+1/(t3−1)+⋯ without end. Chowla asked whether the total is irrational, equal to no fraction of two whole numbers, for every such 𝑡t. The same total is 𝜏(1)/𝑡 +𝜏(2)/𝑡2 +⋯τ(1)/t+τ(2)/t2+⋯, where 𝜏(𝑛)τ(n) is the number of divisors of 𝑛n.

    The statement fixes a rational number 𝑡 >1t>1, that is 𝑡 =𝑎/𝑏t=a/b with whole numbers 𝑎 >𝑏 ≥1a>b≥1; whole numbers count too (𝑏 =1b=1). The value 𝑡 =1t=1 is excluded because the first term 1/(1 −1)1/(1−1) would divide by zero. For each 𝑛 =1,2,3,…n=1,2,3,… the term 1/(𝑡𝑛 −1)1/(tn−1) is a positive fraction, and the question is about the sum of all of them, without end. That sum is finite. Factorising gives

    𝑡𝑛−1=(𝑡−1)(𝑡𝑛−1+⋯+𝑡+1)≥(𝑡−1)𝑡𝑛−1,tn−1=(t−1)(tn−1+⋯+t+1)≥(t−1)tn−1,

    so the 𝑛nth term is at most 1𝑡−1 ⋅1𝑡𝑛−11t−1⋅1tn−1, the 𝑛nth term of a geometric series with ratio 1/𝑡 <11/t<1, and that series has a finite sum.

    In the second form, 𝜏(𝑛)τ(n) counts the whole numbers that divide 𝑛n exactly: 𝜏(6) =4τ(6)=4, from 1, 2, 3 and 6, and 𝜏(𝑝) =2τ(p)=2 for every prime 𝑝p. It is the same total collected by powers of 1/𝑡1/t; the example shows why.

    A number is irrational when it equals no fraction 𝑝/𝑞p/q with whole numbers 𝑝p and 𝑞 ≠0q≠0. The sum of the first 𝑁N terms is always a fraction, so the answer depends on all infinitely many terms together, and a proof must rule out every fraction at once. The usual route is proof by contradiction: suppose the total equals 𝑝/𝑞p/q, and use this to produce a whole number strictly between 0 and 1, which cannot exist.

    The question asks for every rational 𝑡 >1t>1. Erdős settled every whole number 𝑡 ≥2t≥2 in 1948, and some fractions are settled too (see the crux). Among fractions above 1 that are not whole numbers, 3/23/2 has the smallest numerator, and there it is open. Irrational values of 𝑡t are not part of the question.

    An example. At 𝑡 =2t=2 the terms are 1 +1/3 +1/7 +1/15 +⋯1+1/3+1/7+1/15+⋯ and the total is 1.60669…1.60669…; the divisor counts 𝜏(1),…,𝜏(6)τ(1),…,τ(6) are 1, 2, 2, 3, 2, 4. In 1948 Erdős proved the total irrational at every whole number 𝑡 ≥2t≥2. At 𝑡 =3/2t=3/2 the terms are 2 +4/5 +8/19 +⋯2+4/5+8/19+⋯, the total is 3.89715…3.89715…, and whether it is irrational is unknown.

    Here is why divisor counts appear, at 𝑡 =2t=2. A geometric series with first term 1/2𝑛1/2n and ratio 1/2𝑛1/2n adds up to 1/2𝑛1−1/2𝑛 =12𝑛−11/2n1−1/2n=12n−1, so each term of the sum is itself an endless sum of powers of 1/21/2, one row for each 𝑛 =1,2,3,…n=1,2,3,…:

    • 𝑛 =1n=1: 1 =12 +14 +18 +116 +132 +164 +⋯1=12+14+18+116+132+164+⋯
    • 𝑛 =2n=2: 13 =14 +116 +164 +⋯13=14+116+164+⋯
    • 𝑛 =3n=3: 17 =18 +164 +1512 +⋯17=18+164+1512+⋯
    • 𝑛 =4n=4: 115 =116 +1256 +⋯115=116+1256+⋯
    • 𝑛 =5n=5: 131 =132 +11024 +⋯131=132+11024+⋯
    • 𝑛 =6n=6: 163 =164 +14096 +⋯163=164+14096+⋯
    • 𝑛 =7,8,9,…n=7,8,9,…: one row each, starting at 1/2𝑛1/2n.

    Row 𝑛n holds 1/2𝑛,1/22𝑛,1/23𝑛,…1/2n,1/22n,1/23n,…, the powers 1/2𝑘1/2k with 𝑘k a multiple of 𝑛n. So 1/2𝑘1/2k occurs once in row 𝑛n for each 𝑛n that divides 𝑘k, which is 𝜏(𝑘)τ(k) times in all: 1/64 =1/261/64=1/26 occurs in rows 1, 2, 3 and 6, four times, and 𝜏(6) =4τ(6)=4. Every term is positive, so collecting equal powers leaves the total unchanged:

    1+13+17+115+⋯=12+24+28+316+232+464+⋯1+13+17+115+⋯=12+24+28+316+232+464+⋯

    A check with numbers: the six terms shown on the right add to 10064 =1.562510064=1.5625, and the later terms bring the total up to 1.60669…1.60669…, the value of the left side. The same collecting works at every 𝑡 >1t>1 with 1/𝑡1/t in place of 1/21/2, so 𝜏(𝑛)τ(n) is the coefficient of 1/𝑡𝑛1/tn.

    The crux. At a whole-number base 𝑡t, multiplying by 𝑡𝑁tN makes the first 𝑁N terms whole and leaves the base-𝑡t expansion read from place 𝑁N. Erdős showed that expansion has arbitrarily long runs of zero digits and never ends, which no fraction's expansion can do. At 𝑡 =𝑎/𝑏t=a/b the leftover keeps a factor 𝑏𝑁bN: at 3/23/2 it exceeds 2𝑁+12N+1. Built on Zudilin's 2004 forms, the short paper's Theorem 4.1 proves irrationality when 𝑎 >𝑏2.4649…a>b2.4649…, which includes every power of 31/431/4 and excludes 3/23/2.

    Digits. For a whole number 𝑡 ≥2t≥2, base 𝑡t writes a number as a whole part plus 𝑑1/𝑡 +𝑑2/𝑡2 +⋯d1/t+d2/t2+⋯ with digits from 0 to 𝑡 −1t−1; decimals use 𝑡 =10t=10. The second form of the total is such an expansion, with oversized digits 𝜏(𝑛)τ(n) that carrying corrects. Multiplying by 𝑡𝑁tN gives the whole number 𝜏(𝑛) 𝑡𝑁−𝑛τ(n)tN−n from each term with 𝑛 ≤𝑁n≤N and leaves the expansion read from place 𝑁N:

    𝐸𝑁=𝜏(𝑁+1)𝑡+𝜏(𝑁+2)𝑡2+⋯EN=τ(N+1)t+τ(N+2)t2+⋯

    If the total were 𝑝/𝑞p/q, then 𝑞 𝑡𝑁qtN times it would be the whole number 𝑝 𝑡𝑁ptN, so 𝑞 𝐸𝑁qEN is a positive whole number for every 𝑁N; a contradiction needs one strictly between 0 and 1. At 𝑡 =2t=2: 𝐸1 =2 ×1.60669… −𝜏(1) =2.21339…E1=2×1.60669…−τ(1)=2.21339….

    No contradiction yet: in the drawing the base-2 leftover stays between 1 and 5. Erdős's 1948 idea, as the long record summarises it: the Chinese remainder theorem (which finds a number with chosen remainders) gives 𝑁N with 𝜏(𝑁 +1),…,𝜏(𝑁 +𝐿)τ(N+1),…,τ(N+L) divisible by chosen powers of 𝑡t. With the carries controlled, the expansion has arbitrarily long runs of zero digits, and he shows it never ends. A fraction's digits eventually repeat one block, and a zero run longer than the block would make every later digit zero.

    So far, whole-number bases. Next, 𝑡 =𝑎/𝑏t=a/b: now 𝜏(𝑛)/𝑡𝑛 =𝜏(𝑛) 𝑏𝑛/𝑎𝑛τ(n)/tn=τ(n)bn/an, the multiplier is 𝑎𝑁aN, and as every 𝜏 ≥1τ≥1,

    𝐸𝑁=𝑏𝑁(𝜏(𝑁+1)𝑏𝑎+𝜏(𝑁+2)(𝑏𝑎)2+⋯)≥𝑏𝑁+1𝑎−𝑏.EN=bN(τ(N+1)ba+τ(N+2)(ba)2+⋯)≥bN+1a−b.

    The factor 𝑏𝑁bN stays. At 3/23/2 the bound is 2𝑁+12N+1: 𝐸10 =7165.1…E10=7165.1… against 211 =2048211=2048, and the drawing's red points pass 8.5 million at 𝑁 =20N=20. A 𝑞 𝐸𝑁qEN that large is no contradiction. This rules out only this way of clearing; other proofs remain possible.

    A better combination. Zudilin (2004) built combinations 𝑈𝑛(𝑡)𝐹(𝑡) −𝑉𝑛(𝑡)Un(t)F(t)−Vn(t), with whole-number polynomials 𝑈𝑛,𝑉𝑛Un,Vn and 𝐹(𝑡)F(t) the total, that are positive and about 𝑡−221.30…𝑛2t−221.30…n2. The short paper's Theorem 4.1 computes their degree after common factors cancel, about 324.19… 𝑛2324.19…n2, so clearing at 𝑎/𝑏a/b costs a factor 𝑏324.19…𝑛2b324.19…n2. At 31/431/4, 42.4649… =30.48… <3142.4649…=30.48…<31, and equal powers of 31 and 4 keep this; at 3/23/2, 22.4649… =5.52… >322.4649…=5.52…>3.

    Proof idea. Zudilin’s 2004 hypergeometric forms are homogenised at rational bases; common polynomial factors cancel before exact denominator and decay estimates are compared.

    Boundary. The criterion excludes 3/23/2. The universal rational-base question remains open.

    Lean proofComparator checkPaper, Theorem 4.1In the map

    Lean is a programming language for mathematics: a theorem is written in it and a computer checks every step of its proof. Comparator is a separate checking tool: it tests the Lean proof against a statement of the theorem written down on its own, so a proof of a weaker or different statement would fail.

  5. Erdős #249Open

    Is the sum 𝜑(1)/2 +𝜑(2)/4 +𝜑(3)/8 +⋯φ(1)/2+φ(2)/4+φ(3)/8+⋯ irrational?

    Is ∑𝑛𝜙(𝑛)2𝑛∑nϕ(n)2n irrational? Here 𝜙ϕ is the Euler totient function.

    Erdős problem #249, as erdosproblems.com/249 states it

    What it says. Euler’s totient 𝜑(𝑛)φ(n) counts the numbers from 1 to 𝑛n that share no factor greater than 1 with 𝑛n: 𝜑(9) =6φ(9)=6, from 1, 2, 4, 5, 7 and 8. Divide each 𝜑(𝑛)φ(n) by 2𝑛2n and add the results for 𝑛 =1,2,3,…n=1,2,3,…. The question asks whether this total is irrational, that is, equal to no fraction 𝑎/𝑏a/b of whole numbers.

    The sign ∑𝑛∑n means: add the terms for 𝑛 =1,2,3,…n=1,2,3,… without end. The value of an endless sum is the number that its running totals 1/2,3/4,1,9/8,5/4,…1/2,3/4,1,9/8,5/4,… approach; call it 𝑆S. The totient 𝜑(𝑛)φ(n) counts the 𝑘k in {1,2,…,𝑛}{1,2,…,n} whose only common factor with 𝑛n is 1. So 𝜑(1) =1φ(1)=1, 𝜑(6) =2φ(6)=2 (from 1 and 5), and 𝜑(𝑝) =𝑝 −1φ(p)=p−1 for a prime 𝑝p, since no number from 1 to 𝑝 −1p−1 shares a factor greater than 1 with 𝑝p. Always 𝜑(𝑛) ≤𝑛φ(n)≤n.

    So 𝑆S exists and lies between 1 and 2. The first three terms already add to 1, and since 𝜑(𝑛) <𝑛φ(n)<n for 𝑛 ≥2n≥2,

    𝑆<12+24+38+416+⋯=2,S<12+24+38+416+⋯=2,

    where the last sum comes from differentiating 1 +𝑥 +𝑥2 +⋯ =1/(1 −𝑥)1+x+x2+⋯=1/(1−x), multiplying by 𝑥x and putting 𝑥 =1/2x=1/2.

    Irrational means that 𝑆S equals no fraction 𝑎/𝑏a/b with whole numbers 𝑎a and 𝑏 ≥1b≥1. Every running total is a fraction with a power of 2 below the line, such as 87/6487/64 after ten terms, so the question concerns the endless sum only. A proof must rule out every 𝑏b at once. Computing 𝑆S to many places rules out each 𝑏b up to some bound and never all of them: the long record rules out every denominator up to about 7.96 ×10347.96×1034, and the question is still open.

    An example. Since 𝜑(1) =𝜑(2) =1φ(1)=φ(2)=1, 𝜑(3) =𝜑(4) =2φ(3)=φ(4)=2 and 𝜑(5) =4φ(5)=4, the sum begins 1/2 +1/4 +2/8 +2/16 +4/32 +⋯1/2+1/4+2/8+2/16+4/32+⋯. These five terms add to exactly 5/45/4; ten terms give 87/64 =1.35937587/64=1.359375. The whole sum is 𝑆 =1.36763…S=1.36763…, in binary 1.0101111000011101…21.0101111000011101…2. The term 𝜑(11)/211φ(11)/211, with 𝜑(11) =10 =10102φ(11)=10=10102, has its binary digits in places 8 to 11 after the point.

    Binary places work like decimal places with 2 in place of 10: a digit 𝑘k places after the point is worth 1/2𝑘1/2k, so 1.012 =1 +0/2 +1/4 =5/41.012=1+0/2+1/4=5/4. Dividing a whole number by 2𝑛2n moves its binary point 𝑛n places to the left. For example 𝜑(11) =10 =10102φ(11)=10=10102, so

    𝜑(11)211=0.000000010102=128+1210.φ(11)211=0.000000010102=128+1210.

    The last digit of 𝜑(𝑛)φ(n) always lands in place 𝑛n. The first five terms in binary, added in columns as in the drawing, are

    0.12+0.012+0.012+0.0012+0.0012=1.012=5/4.0.12+0.012+0.012+0.0012+0.0012=1.012=5/4.
    1. Place 3 holds two 1s, from 𝑛 =4n=4 and 𝑛 =5n=5: 1 +1 =1021+1=102, so write 0 and carry 1 into place 2.
    2. Place 2 holds two 1s, from 𝑛 =2n=2 and 𝑛 =3n=3, and the carry: 1 +1 +1 =1121+1+1=112, so write 1 and carry 1 into place 1.
    3. Place 1 holds the 1 from 𝑛 =1n=1 and the carry: 1 +1 =1021+1=102, so write 0 and carry 1 into the units.

    Later terms keep changing earlier digits. Ten terms give 87/64 =1.0101110000287/64=1.01011100002. The terms after the tenth add

    𝑅10=𝜑(11)2+𝜑(12)4+⋯=8.45…R10=φ(11)2+φ(12)4+⋯=8.45…

    units of place 10. Eight units of place 10 make one unit of place 7, so the 0 in place 7 turns into a 1, and 𝑆S begins 1.0101111000…21.0101111000…2. In general the terms after the 𝑁Nth add 𝑅𝑁RN units of place 𝑁N, so the digit in place 𝑁N depends on terms far beyond the 𝑁Nth.

    The crux. In binary, 𝜑(𝑛)/2𝑛φ(n)/2n is the whole number 𝜑(𝑛)φ(n) written so that its last digit sits in place 𝑛n after the point. Neighbouring terms overlap, and adding them carries digits from place to place. Proofs that work when the numerators stay small fail here, because 𝜑(𝑛) =𝑛 −1φ(n)=n−1 whenever 𝑛n is prime. Changing 𝜑(𝑛)φ(n) by at most 2 at even 𝑛n (the ringed digits) gives a sum of exactly 5/45/4.

    What a proof must show. Long division of 𝑎a by 𝑞q in binary gives one digit per step and leaves a remainder from 0 to 𝑞 −1q−1, so within 𝑞 +1q+1 steps a remainder repeats and the digits repeat from then on: for 1/51/5 the remainders run 1,2,4,3,1,…1,2,4,3,1,… and 1/5 =0.0011 0011…21/5=0.00110011…2. Conversely, eventually repeating digits give a fraction, so 𝑆S is irrational exactly when its digits never settle into a repeating block.

    Small numerators. Replace 𝜑(𝑛)φ(n) by its remainder on division by 𝑚 ≥3m≥3. If that sum were 𝑎/𝑞a/q, its 𝑅𝑁RN, each 2𝑁𝑎/𝑞2Na/q minus a whole number, would be whole or at least 1/𝑞1/q from whole. Primes give arbitrarily long stretches of 𝑛n with remainder 0, then nonzero remainders. Just before a stretch of length 𝐿L, 0 <𝑅𝑁 ≤(𝑚 −1)/2𝐿0<RN≤(m−1)/2L, its value if every later remainder were 𝑚 −1m−1, so 𝑅𝑁 <1/𝑞RN<1/q once 𝐿L is long. Hence that sum is irrational for every 𝑚 ≥3m≥3 (the short paper; also Erdős 1957).

    So far: a fraction keeps each 𝑅𝑁RN whole or at least 1/𝑞1/q from whole, and long zero stretches break that. Next: 𝜑(𝑛)φ(n) itself.

    with ∑𝑐(𝑛)/2𝑛 =5/4 =1.012∑c(n)/2n=5/4=1.012, the ember row. Each 𝑐(𝑛)c(n) lies between 0 and 𝑛n and within 2 of 𝜑(𝑛)φ(n). So any argument using only such rough information would prove 5/45/4 irrational. A proof needs exact laws of 𝜑φ, such as 𝜑(4𝑛) =2𝜑(2𝑛)φ(4n)=2φ(2n), which 𝑐c breaks at 𝑛 =1n=1.

    What is proved. Digits repeating in blocks of ℎh make 𝑅𝑁+ℎ −𝑅𝑁RN+h−RN whole for all large 𝑁N. So 𝑆S is irrational exactly when each ℎh has arbitrarily late 𝑁N where this difference falls strictly between whole numbers. One route to them needs two cancellation estimates for sums built from 𝜑φ (the short paper), both unproved. Erdős’s question is open.

    The interesting resultExact classification

    A totient-remainder series is rational exactly when even remainders score alike

    Euler’s totient from 543 to 551, divided by 8: the prime 547 leaves remainder 2, its eight neighbours 0. Score remainder 2 as 1, 6 as −1 and the rest 0, and give the score at 𝑛n the weight 2−𝑛2−n. If the sum were a fraction with denominator 15, 15 times its tail after 542 would be a whole number, one of these marks. Each zero before 547 halves the tail’s possible range; after four, only the mark 0 remains. The 1 pushes it off 0; each zero after it halves what unseen scores could cancel, leaving it strictly between 0 and 1. Such windows exist at every length, so the sum is irrational unless all even remainders score alike, say 𝑐c; then this tail is exactly 𝑐c.

    The rows list 𝑛n, 𝜑(𝑛)φ(n) and 𝜑(𝑛)mod8φ(n)mod8; 547 ≡3(mod8)547≡3(mod8) is prime, so 𝜑(547) =546 ≡2φ(547)=546≡2. The key scores the even residues 0,2,4,60,2,4,6 as 0,1,0, −10,1,0,−1 and the odd ones 0, so 𝑆 =∑𝑎𝑛2−𝑛S=∑an2−n with |𝑎𝑛| ≤1|an|≤1. Cut after 542: 𝑈 =∑𝑡≥1𝑎542+𝑡2−𝑡 =2542𝑆 −∑𝑛≤542𝑎𝑛2542−𝑛U=∑t≥1a542+t2−t=2542S−∑n≤542an2542−n, so 𝑆 =𝑏/15S=b/15 would make 15𝑈15U an integer. Each bar is the exact range of 15𝑈15U given the scores down to its row: four left zeros give |15𝑈| ≤15/16|15U|≤15/16, and with 𝑈 =2−5(1 +2−4𝑉)U=2−5(1+2−4V), |𝑉| ≤1|V|≤1, the right zeros give 15𝑈 ∈[225/512,255/512] ⊂(0,1)15U∈[225/512,255/512]⊂(0,1). This is Lemma 4.2 read at one cut; the same window rules out every denominator up to 30. The proof of Theorem 4.1 supplies, by the Chinese remainder and Dirichlet theorems, a prime centre with any even residue and any number of zero neighbours, so the series is rational exactly when the even scores agree, and its value is then 3𝑓(1)/4 +𝑐/43f(1)/4+c/4. The irrationality of ∑𝜑(𝑛)/2𝑛∑φ(n)/2n remains open.

    Write 𝜑φ for Euler’s totient. For 𝑘 ≥1k≥1 and 𝑓:ℤ/2𝑘ℤ →ℚf:Z/2kZ→Q, ∑𝑛≥1𝑓(𝜑(𝑛)mod2𝑘)2𝑛∑n≥1f(φ(n)mod2k)2n is rational exactly when 𝑓f is constant on the even residue classes. If that constant is 𝑐c, the value is 3𝑓(1)4 +𝑐43f(1)4+c4. Also, ∑𝜑(𝑛)mod𝑚2𝑛∑φ(n)modm2n is irrational for every 𝑚 ≥3m≥3.

    Proof idea. Congruence constructions isolate a nonzero totient residue between long zero blocks. Bounded tails then conflict with rationality’s fixed denominator.

    Boundary. This classifies bounded residue observables. Irrationality of the series with unreduced totients remains open.

    Lean proofComparator checkPaper §4In the map

    Lean is a programming language for mathematics: a theorem is written in it and a computer checks every step of its proof. Comparator is a separate checking tool: it tests the Lean proof against a statement of the theorem written down on its own, so a proof of a weaker or different statement would fail.

  6. Erdős #251Open

    Is 2/2 +3/4 +5/8 +7/16 +⋯2/2+3/4+5/8+7/16+⋯, primes over powers of two, irrational?

    Is ∑𝑝𝑛2𝑛∑pn2n irrational? (Here 𝑝𝑛pn is the 𝑛nth prime.)

    Erdős problem #251, as erdosproblems.com/251 states it

    What it says. Here 𝑝𝑛pn is the 𝑛n-th prime: 𝑝1 =2p1=2, 𝑝2 =3p2=3, 𝑝3 =5p3=5, 𝑝4 =7p4=7, and so on. The 𝑛n-th term is 𝑝𝑛pn divided by 2𝑛2n, and the sum adds the terms for every 𝑛 =1,2,3,…n=1,2,3,…. The question asks whether the total is irrational, that is, equal to no fraction 𝑎/𝑏a/b of whole numbers.

    The primes are the whole numbers above 1 whose only divisors are 1 and themselves, in increasing order: 2,3,5,7,11,13,…2,3,5,7,11,13,…. The symbol 𝑝𝑛pn is the 𝑛n-th of them, so 𝑝5 =11p5=11 and 𝑝10 =29p10=29. The power 2𝑛2n is 2 multiplied by itself 𝑛n times, so the fifth term is 𝑝5/25 =11/32p5/25=11/32. The sign ∑∑ with no limits written means: add the terms for 𝑛 =1,2,3,…n=1,2,3,… without end. Numbering from 𝑛 =0n=0 (2/1 +3/2 +5/4 +⋯2/1+3/2+5/4+⋯) doubles the total and leaves the question unchanged.

    The partial sums (the first term, the first two, the first three, and so on) approach one number. The long record derives the bound 𝑝𝑛 ≤1250 𝑛4pn≤1250n4 from an elementary argument of Erdős (1932), while 2𝑛2n doubles at each step. From 𝑛 =10n=10 on, each bound 1250 𝑛4/2𝑛1250n4/2n is less than 3/43/4 of the one before, so the remaining terms add to less than a geometric series, and the partial sums, which only increase, settle on one number.

    A number is rational when it equals a fraction 𝑎/𝑏a/b of whole numbers with 𝑏 ≠0b≠0, such as 101/32101/32, and irrational when no such fraction equals it. Every partial sum is rational. Replacing finitely many of the primes by other whole numbers changes the total by a fraction, and adding a fraction never changes whether a number is a fraction. So the answer depends only on the primes far out, and a proof must show that no fraction whatever equals the total.

    Computation alone cannot do this. A finite calculation traps the total in a short interval, and that excludes every fraction with a small denominator: the long record proves, by exact integer arithmetic checked in the Lean proof assistant, that a fraction equal to the sum would need a denominator above 10120401012040. Every interval also contains fractions with larger denominators, so no finite calculation can exclude them all.

    An example. The first five terms are 2/2 +3/4 +5/8 +7/16 +11/322/2+3/4+5/8+7/16+11/32. Over the common denominator 32 they add to (32 +24 +20 +14 +11)/32 =101/32 =3.15625(32+24+20+14+11)/32=101/32=3.15625. The later terms shrink quickly, because 2𝑛2n doubles at each step while the primes grow far more slowly, and the whole sum is 3.67464…3.67464… to five decimal places.

    Put every term over the denominator 32 by multiplying its top and bottom by 16, 8, 4, 2 and 1:

    22+34+58+716+1132=32+24+20+14+1132=10132=3+532=3.1562522+34+58+716+1132=32+24+20+14+1132=10132=3+532=3.15625

    The next terms, 13/64,17/128,19/256,23/512,…13/64,17/128,19/256,23/512,…, are each smaller than the one before, since the denominator doubles and the next prime is less than twice the last. The partial sums for 𝑛 =1,2,…,9n=1,2,…,9 are

    1, 1.75, 2.375, 2.8125, 3.15625, 3.359375, 3.4921875, 3.56640625, 3.611328125, …1, 1.75, 2.375, 2.8125, 3.15625, 3.359375, 3.4921875, 3.56640625, 3.611328125, …

    and they increase towards 3.67464…3.67464… without reaching it.

    The crux works with the gaps between consecutive primes: 3 −2 =13−2=1, 5 −3 =25−3=2, 7 −5 =27−5=2, 11 −7 =411−7=4, and so on, giving 1,2,2,4,2,4,2,4,6,2,…1,2,2,4,2,4,2,4,6,2,…. Every prime is 2 plus the gaps before it, for example 11 =2 +1 +2 +2 +411=2+1+2+2+4.

    Here is the move behind the short paper's theorem. Add 6 in all to the third and fourth gaps, 2 and 4, split as 0 +60+6, 2 +42+4, 4 +24+2 or 6 +06+0. In the gap sum 2 +1/2 +2/4 +2/8 +4/16 +⋯2+1/2+2/4+2/8+4/16+⋯ of the crux these gaps carry the weights 1/81/8 and 1/161/16, so the four splits raise it by

    08+616=616,28+416=816,48+216=1016,68+016=1216.08+616=616,28+416=816,48+216=1016,68+016=1216.

    Each changed gap rises by an even amount, so it stays even. Every number built after the pair, 2 plus the gaps so far, rises by exactly 6: 11,13,17,19,…11,13,17,19,… are replaced by 17,19,23,25,…17,19,23,25,…, each keeping its remainder on division by 2, by 3 and by 6. Yet the four splits move the sum by four different amounts. The new numbers need not be prime: 25 is not.

    The crux. Each prime is 2 plus the gaps before it, so the sum equals 2 +∑𝑛≥1(𝑝𝑛+1 −𝑝𝑛)/2𝑛2+∑n≥1(pn+1−pn)/2n, as Tao noted. The gaps 1,2,2,4,2,4,…1,2,2,4,2,4,… are even after the first and never settle into a repeating cycle. The short paper shows that rare small changes to the gaps, which from some point on leave the remainder of every gap and of every prime on division by any fixed number unchanged, still move the sum to every value in an interval, fractions included.

    The classical test. Write a number between 0 and 1 in binary by doubling: the whole part of each double is the next digit, and the fractional part is kept. For a fraction with denominator 𝑏b, each fractional part is one of 0/𝑏,…,(𝑏 −1)/𝑏0/b,…,(b−1)/b, so within 𝑏b doublings one recurs and the digits repeat from there. For 7/127/12:

    712→212 (digit 1)→412 (0)→812 (0)→412 (1)→812 (0)→⋯712→212 (digit 1)→412 (0)→812 (0)→412 (1)→812 (0)→⋯

    so 7/12 =0.10010101…7/12=0.10010101… in binary. Hence a number whose binary digits never settle into a repeating cycle is irrational. Here the primes over 2,4,8,…2,4,8,… exceed the digits 0 and 1 and carry into earlier places (3/4 =1/2 +1/43/4=1/2+1/4), so the sum's digits cannot be read off.

    The gap form. Write each prime as 2 plus the gaps before it. The 2 sits in every prime and contributes 2/2 +2/4 +2/8 +⋯ =22/2+2/4+2/8+⋯=2. The gap 2 from 3 to 5 sits in 5,7,11,…5,7,11,…, so it contributes 2/8 +2/16 +2/32 +⋯ =2/42/8+2/16+2/32+⋯=2/4: the first 𝑘k terms of 1/8 +1/16 +⋯1/8+1/16+⋯ fall short of 1/41/4 by the last of them. Likewise the gap after 𝑝𝑛pn contributes (𝑝𝑛+1 −𝑝𝑛)/2𝑛(pn+1−pn)/2n. All pieces are positive, so regrouping keeps the total:

    22+34+58+716+⋯=2+12+24+28+416+⋯22+34+58+716+⋯=2+12+24+28+416+⋯

    In the drawing, columns give the left side and rows the right. So far: the sum is a fraction exactly when the gap sum is.

    The short paper's limit. Repeat the example's move at places ever farther apart, in multiples of 2 ⋅3⋯𝑘2⋅3⋯k for growing 𝑘k, leaving any first stretch of gaps unchanged. The changed gaps keep:

    • each change far out is at most log⁡(𝑛 +3)log⁡(n+3) at the 𝑛n-th gap, on places whose share of long stretches shrinks to 0;
    • for each fixed whole number 𝑞q, from some point on, every gap and running total (2 plus the gaps so far) keeps its remainder on division by 𝑞q;
    • each pattern of consecutive gaps, such as 2, 4, 2, keeps its frequency up to an error tending to 0;
    • the running totals still grow like 𝑛log⁡𝑛nlog⁡n.

    Yet the changed sums take every value in an interval, fractions included, so these facts alone cannot prove irrationality. The running totals need not be prime, so a proof must use finer facts about the primes. Land's draft proves irrationality assuming a strong unproved conjecture on prime patterns (a uniform Hardy–Littlewood conjecture), along a route Tao suggested. Unconditionally the problem is open.

    The interesting resultLimitation of a proof method

    Sparse congruence-preserving corrections fill an interval

    Share six added units between neighbouring entries, in packets of two. In the dyadic sum every unit counts once, earlier ones once more: 6 +2 =86+2=8. Move a packet earlier: 6 +4 =106+4=10. Six units still pass onward, so later congruences are unchanged. The construction’s first group shares 30: 30 +14 =4430+14=44. Each split leaves a window, the totals later groups can still add. One more packet earlier gives 30 +16 =4630+16=46 and slides the window one step. Later groups can add at least one step, so neighbouring windows overlap: the sixteen leave no gap. Choose the window holding the target; inside it, the next group’s 32 windows meet end to end. Repeat: the windows close on the target, so the sum equals it. Corrected prime gaps need not be prime gaps; the prime series remains open.

    Upper left, the cumulative correction 𝐸𝑚 =∑𝑖<𝑚𝑒𝑖Em=∑i<mei over a dyadic ruler, slot 𝑚m of width 2−𝑚−12−m−1, so the area is ∑𝑒𝑛2−𝑛−1 =∑𝐸𝑚2−𝑚−1∑en2−n−1=∑Em2−m−1. One stage of the short paper’s §2 construction, with 𝑓(𝑛) =𝑛f(n)=n and initial index 188: 𝑀0 =2M0=2, 𝐷0 =15D0=15, (𝑒192,𝑒193) =(2𝑑,30 −2𝑑)(e192,e193)=(2d,30−2d), so the area is (30 +2𝑑)2−194(30+2d)2−194; raising 𝐸193E193 by 2 adds 𝑤0 =2−193w0=2−193, and 𝐸194 =30E194=30 for every 𝑑d. Upper right, row 𝑑d is the window [𝐿,𝑈] =[𝐵 +𝑑𝑤0,𝐵 +𝑑𝑤0 +𝐹1][L,U]=[B+dw0,B+dw0+F1], 𝐵B the all-later total and 𝐹1 =∑𝑖≥1𝐷𝑖𝑤𝑖F1=∑i≥1Diwi; 𝐹1/𝑤0 =3 +18 ⋅2−1346 +⋯F1/w0=3+18⋅2−1346+⋯, and by equation (3), 𝐹𝑗+1 ≥𝑤𝑗Fj+1≥wj, the union is [𝐵,𝐵 +𝐹0][B,B+F0]. Below, the window holding 𝐵 +(8 +93160)𝑤0B+(8+93160)w0 enlarged by 32/332/3, then twice by 32: above its lower end, the next group’s windows [𝑑𝑤𝑗+1,𝑑𝑤𝑗+1 +𝐹𝑗+2][dwj+1,dwj+1+Fj+2], 1 <𝐹𝑗+2/𝑤𝑗+1 <1 +2−13001<Fj+2/wj+1<1+2−1300, tile it, and the target takes 6, 6, then 12. The covering step is Crmarić and Kovač’s Lemma 4; the support, the interval and every modulus cutoff are fixed before the target (Proposition 1.1). The Lean proof uses a construction changing one coordinate per stage (§7).

    Let 𝑎𝑛an be nonnegative integers with 𝐴 =∑𝑛≥0𝑎𝑛2𝑛+1A=∑n≥0an2n+1 finite, and let 𝑓(𝑛) →∞f(n)→∞. Corrections 0 ≤𝑒𝑛 ≤𝑓(𝑛)0≤en≤f(n) eventually, supported on one set of upper Banach density zero, make ∑𝑛≥0𝑎𝑛+𝑒𝑛2𝑛+1∑n≥0an+en2n+1 fill a nondegenerate interval above 𝐴A. For every fixed modulus, 𝑒𝑛en and its cumulative sums eventually vanish modulo it.

    Proof idea. Spaced blocks encode arbitrary target digits; factorial divisibility preserves all fixed congruences while block spacing makes the support sparse.

    Boundary. Applied to prime gaps this produces comparison sequences, not primes. Irrationality of the actual prime-value dyadic series remains open.

  7. Erdős #269Open

    Do the reciprocals of running least common multiples sum to an irrational?

    Let 𝑃P be a finite set of primes with |𝑃| ≥2|P|≥2 and let {𝑎1 <𝑎2 <⋯} ={𝑛 ∈ℕ :if 𝑝 ∣𝑛 then 𝑝 ∈𝑃}{a1<a2<⋯}={n∈N:if p∣n then p∈P}. Is the sum ∑∞𝑛=11[𝑎1,…,𝑎𝑛],∑n=1∞1[a1,…,an], where [𝑎1,…,𝑎𝑛][a1,…,an] is the lowest common multiple of 𝑎1,…,𝑎𝑛a1,…,an, irrational?

    Erdős problem #269, as erdosproblems.com/269 states it

    What it says. List, in increasing order, the positive whole numbers whose prime factors all lie in 𝑃P, starting with 1, which has none; for 𝑃 ={2,3}P={2,3} the list is 1,2,3,4,6,8,9,12,…1,2,3,4,6,8,9,12,…. The bracket [𝑎1,…,𝑎𝑛][a1,…,an] is the least common multiple of the first 𝑛n of them. The question asks whether the reciprocals of these running least common multiples add up to an irrational number.

    Read the statement symbol by symbol. 𝑃P is a finite set of primes, at least two of them, such as {2,3}{2,3} or {2,3,5}{2,3,5}. The set in braces holds every positive whole number 𝑛n whose prime divisors all belong to 𝑃P. It is infinite, since it contains every power of each prime in 𝑃P, and 𝑎1 <𝑎2 <𝑎3 <⋯a1<a2<a3<⋯ lists it in increasing order.

    The bracket is the least common multiple: the smallest positive whole number that each of 𝑎1,…,𝑎𝑛a1,…,an divides. For example [4,6] =12[4,6]=12. It is a running least common multiple, recomputed each time one more number joins, so the sum has one term for every position in the list, and equal terms are all counted.

    Irrational means equal to no fraction 𝐴/𝐷A/D of whole numbers. A proof must rule out every denominator 𝐷D at once, and no amount of computed decimal places can do that.

    The question is asked for every finite set of at least two primes. With one prime the sum is rational: for 𝑃 ={2}P={2} the list is 1,2,4,8,…1,2,4,8,…, the running least common multiple of the first 𝑛n numbers is 2𝑛−12n−1, and

    1+12+14+18+⋯=2.1+12+14+18+⋯=2.

    For an infinite set of primes, Erdős and Graham record that the sum is irrational. Two primes are settled, as the crux explains; three or more primes are open.

    An example. For 𝑃 ={2,3,5}P={2,3,5} the first ten numbers are 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10, 12, and their running least common multiples are 1, 2, 6, 12, 60, 60, 120, 360, 360, 360. These ten terms add up to 9/59/5, and the whole sum is 1.8093 to four decimal places.

    Each new number either already divides the current multiple, which then stays the same, or brings one more prime factor. In the summary, 6 =2 ×36=2×3 already divides 60, so the multiple stays 60; 8 =238=23 needs a third factor 2, so it is 60 ×2 =12060×2=120. Grouping equal terms over the common denominator 360:

    1+12+16+112+260+1120+3360=360+180+60+30+12+3+33601+12+16+112+260+1120+3360=360+180+60+30+12+3+3360 =648360=95.=648360=95.

    Counting each distinct multiple once instead gives

    1+12+16+112+160+1120+1360=640360=169.1+12+16+112+160+1120+1360=640360=169.

    The two differ by 8/360 =1/458/360=1/45: the second copy of 1/601/60 and the extra two copies of 1/3601/360.

    The runs lengthen. From 16 to 31 the list holds 16, 18, 20, 24, 25, 27, 30, with running least common multiples 720, 720, 720, 720, 3600, 10800, 10800, so this stretch adds 4/720 +1/3600 +2/108004/720+1/3600+2/10800. All sixteen numbers of the list from 256 to 500 share the running least common multiple 28 ×35 ×53 =777600028×35×53=7776000.

    The sum is finite. From 2𝑎2a to just below 2𝑎+12a+1 the list holds at most (𝑎 +1)2(a+1)2 numbers: the exponents of 3 and 5 are each at most 𝑎a, giving (𝑎 +1)2(a+1)2 choices, and each choice leaves room for at most one power of 2, since doubling leaves the range. Each of their terms is at most 1/2𝑎1/2a, because 2𝑎2a is already in the list. These bounds add up to ∑𝑎≥0(𝑎 +1)2/2𝑎 =12∑a≥0(a+1)2/2a=12. Computed exactly below 240240, with the same bound for the rest, the sum is 1.8093 to four decimal places.

    The crux. The running least common multiple changes only at prime powers, so equal terms come in runs. Counted once per run, the {2,3,5}{2,3,5} sum is irrational: the short paper proves this case of Erdős's 1973 assertion by a long-division argument. Kept, the run lengths make the remainders of that argument grow without bound, and the question stays open. For two primes, Steve Fan showed in a public post that the sum is transcendental: a root of no polynomial with whole-number coefficients.

    Why the terms come in runs. The running least common multiple up to 𝑥x is the product of the largest power of each prime of 𝑃P not above 𝑥x; up to 24 it is 16 ×9 ×5 =72016×9×5=720. A number up to 𝑥x splits into prime powers (24 =8 ×324=8×3) that are in the list and share no prime, so it already divides that product. Only a prime power changes the multiple, by one more factor of its prime. For {2,3,5}{2,3,5} the changes come at 2,3,4,5,8,9,16,25,27,32,…2,3,4,5,8,9,16,25,27,32,…: the staircase's risers; its treads are the runs.

    The model: long division. Dividing 1 by 7 leaves remainders 1,3,2,6,4,5,1,…1,3,2,6,4,5,1,…; each fixes the next digit and remainder, so with six nonzero remainders the digits 142857 must repeat for ever.

    Counted once per run. Cut the sum before a number of the list and multiply the rest, the tail, by the running least common multiple 𝐿L at the cut. If the sum were 𝐴/𝐷A/D, 𝐷D times this scaled tail would be whole, as each earlier multiple divides 𝐿L. Each later distinct multiple at least doubles, so the scaled tail lies between 0 and 1: finitely many values, like the remainders. For {2,3,5}{2,3,5} the short paper proves a tail fixes the jumps up to the next power of 2 and the next tail, so a repeat would make the jumps periodic: 𝑐c powers of 3 in every ℓℓ stretches between powers of 2. Counting powers of 3 below 2𝑛ℓ2nℓ, 𝑛n large, forces 2ℓ =3𝑐2ℓ=3c, impossible since one is even and one odd. Erdős asserted this for every such 𝑃P in a letter of 1 January 1973 that prints no proof.

    Where it stops. So far, finitely many tails force a repeat. Kept, runs add weight: multiplied by 360, the stretch from 16 to 31 gives 4 ⋅360720 +3603600 +2 ⋅36010800 =1364⋅360720+3603600+2⋅36010800=136; the long record's bounds give the stretch from 2𝑎2a at least 𝑎2/450a2/450. The scaled tails contain these stretches, so they grow without bound, and 𝐷D times them, whole numbers without a ceiling, need never repeat.

    What is known. The short paper recasts irrationality as an equivalent remainder test, still unproved. For two primes, Fan split the sum into a product of two sums and deduced transcendence from a theorem of Loxton and van der Poorten; for three primes the short paper proves no such finite splitting exists.

    The interesting resultLimitation of a proof method

    Three-prime LCM kernels have nonzero minors of every order

    With primes 2 and 3 only, Steve Fan’s factorisation makes the table of reciprocal running LCMs one copied row: the second is half the first. Allow 5: the running LCM at cutoff 6 is 60; the copy predicts 1/121/12, the table holds 1/601/60. Dividing every entry by its one-row prediction leaves only 1 and 1/51/5. A column stands at the factor its label needs to reach a power of 5; a row reads 1/51/5 where its own factor suffices. Subtracting neighbouring rows leaves one interval each, and one column lands in each interval. Row 8, at 8/58/5, splits an interval; column 81, at 125/81125/81, detects the new piece. Columns fall in every gap, so no finite sum ∑ℓ𝑓ℓ(𝑖)𝐺ℓ(𝑗,𝑘)∑ℓfℓ(i)Gℓ(j,k) equals the kernel. Whether the sum is irrational stays open.

CodeMap and Agent Trace are private. The #257 film explains Erdős’s 1968 reciprocal-summability criterion; the unrestricted question remains open. Its Palomar comment is outdated: a weighted-support edition was registered on 25 September 2026. Current registration record.

Why I am building it

I expect models to improve at maths. Human experts will still need to check their results.

On 6 October 2026 OpenAI released 722 manuscripts produced by an internal model.

I was vibe-mathing back in early 2025, and even then I realised formal verification is necessary but not sufficient for a lay person wanting to use AI to do maths. It’s necessary because I can’t check a proof myself, so Lean is how I know a statement is actually proved. It isn’t sufficient because Lean won’t tell you whether a statement is the one you meant, whether it was worth asking, or whether anyone can follow why it’s true. Philosophers and mathematicians wrote about exactly this in September, De Toffoli and Duede on logical versus intelligible proof, and Henry Cohn on unexplained AI proofs as technical debt that somebody else has to pay.

So I chose eight hard Erdős problems, went very deep into them, and set each one out like a funnel. The long papers keep the investigation, including the routes that failed and why we think they failed, and the short papers pick out what matters and ground it in the literature. The map traces each checked theorem to where it sits in the papers, I demonstrate the maths and software in the videos, and The eight problems sets out each problem as Erdős posed it, draws its crux and keeps one interesting result under it.

The software has the same problem: my system for running AI agents has far more moving parts than I can keep in my head, so I built a front end over it. CodeMap goes from the whole architecture down to one file and its connections, Agent Trace follows Claude Code and Codex as they work, and Demo Take edits my recordings into videos. The system map shows 88 components from it, released as the earlier software, and the safety doctrine they follow.

I would like mathematicians to suggest research directions and review the papers. This has been difficult to arrange, so the current system is a proof of concept.

The longer account: how this started and what I am trying to do

  • A smaller source brief (JSON) keeps paper text, glossary and guides.

For AI readers and coding agents

JSON is a structured text format an assistant can search by paper, problem, term or source path. No coding app is needed to read it. Each download is a snapshot of the public material, with source references; it does not contain the complete Git repositories, PDF files or video files. Use the links for those. Reading a recorded check does not rerun it.

Setup prompt for a coding agent

A mathematics task needs only the mathematics repository. A software task needs only the software repository. This prompt is for an assessment across both.

My task is [describe the question or change]. Use https://github.com/wcook04/plectis for software components and https://github.com/wcook04/plectis-erdos for mathematics and Lean proofs. Clone the repository my task needs from current main; use both only if the task crosses them. Preserve any existing local work. Read README.md and the compact agent entry: AGENTS.override.md where present, otherwise AGENTS.md. Record the checkout commit and local changes. For mathematics, use python3 scripts/agent_entry.py --entry with my task, and --checkout --check-upstream to compare with public main. For software, follow QUICKSTART.md and run the quickstart check or selected component example, saving output under .microcosm/. Do the task and return source paths, exact commands and outcomes, and the remaining assumptions or unresolved step. Report anything you could not run as not established, never as false. A release tag is a frozen edition, not current main.

The coding-agent guide walks through each step

Take part

If you have a correction, a mathematical idea or a software improvement, send me the specific point. You don’t have to implement it yourself, and I’ll credit your contribution with your permission. If you prove a result, I won’t claim any priority for it and the result is yours.

Email me Work on a problem Credit policy

Or email me about research collaboration, a partnership or licence, or just a conversation about the work. The contact page lists the other routes, from checking a claim to reusing the source.
